task_description: I need to email our dermatologists about a new insurance pre-authorization requirement that adds 48 hours to certain procedure approvals — it affects their scheduling.

rubric_used.user_goals_summary: Writes clinic communications that prioritize patient safety and workflow continuity. Every process change is communicated with both the ideal flow and the fallback when things break. Treats email as a non-secure channel at all times.

rubric.name: Patient Flow Impact First
rubric.description: Changes are explained through their impact on patient experience and flow before the operational rationale. How many extra minutes per appointment, which rooms are affected, what the patient sees differently.

dimensions.label: The first substantive paragraph describes how the change affects patient experience or flow
Includes specific time estimates for how the change affects appointment duration or wait times
The business or compliance reason for the change appears after the patient impact, not before

rubric.name: Fallback Procedures Included
rubric.description: Every new process includes an explicit fallback for when the primary method fails. Clinical settings can't pause when technology breaks — staff need to know what to do when the system is down.

dimensions.label: Includes a specific 'if X fails, do Y instead' instruction
The fallback is a concrete procedure, not 'contact IT' or 'notify your manager'
Names the specific failure scenario the fallback addresses (system down, connectivity loss, etc.)

rubric.name: No Patient Identifiers
rubric.description: Never references patients by name in any email, even internal ones. Uses case numbers, room references, or appointment times. Email is treated as a non-secure channel regardless of policy.

dimensions.label: Does not include any patient names, initials, or uniquely identifying information
Refers to patients by case number, room number, appointment time, or generic reference
Does not include specific diagnoses, treatments, or medical details that could identify a patient in context

rubric.name: Bounded Process Steps
rubric.description: Multi-step processes use numbered steps, capped at 5. If a process needs more than 5 steps to explain in email, it needs a training session — the email should announce the training, not attempt to replace it.

dimensions.label: Processes with more than two actions use numbered steps
No process in the email exceeds 5 numbered steps
If a process is too complex for 5 steps, the email schedules training instead of attempting full documentation

rubric_used.coaching_notes: James's non-negotiable: every new process has a fallback. In clinical settings, 'the system is down' is not an edge case, it's a Tuesday. Will reject any email that names a patient or introduces a process without explaining what to do when it breaks.

rounds.draft:
**Subject: Pre-Authorization Timeline Change — Scheduling Impact Starting [Date]**

---

**To:** Dermatology Clinical Team
**From:** [Your Name/Department]
**Date:** [Date]

---

Effective [date], certain procedures will require a 48-hour pre-authorization window before scheduling can be confirmed with patients. This means appointments that previously could be booked within the same week may now need an additional two business days built into the timeline. Patients arriving for affected procedure types will need to have authorization confirmed before their visit is finalized — front desk staff will flag any gaps at check-in, and same-day scheduling for these procedures will no longer be available as a default option.

This change is driven by updated requirements from several major payers, who have added prior authorization steps for a subset of dermatologic procedures. A full list of affected procedure codes is attached. If you have questions about which specific cases fall under the new requirement, please reach out to the billing team directly rather than including case details in email.

**Updated Scheduling Process**

1. At time of referral or appointment request, front desk confirms whether the procedure code requires pre-auth using the attached reference list.
2. If pre-auth is required, the authorization request is submitted through [system name] before the appointment is booked.
3. Front desk holds the appointment slot for 48 hours pending confirmation.
4. Once authorization is received, the appointment is confirmed with the patient.
5. If authorization is denied or delayed beyond 48 hours, the scheduling team notifies the provider to determine next steps.

**If the Authorization System Is Unavailable**

If [system name] is down or inaccessible, do not hold patients in an unconfirmed status. Instead, submit the authorization request by fax to the payer using the backup forms kept in the front desk binder (updated copies distributed [date]). Document the fax confirmation number in the paper log and flag the appointment in the scheduling system as "pending — manual auth" once access is restored. This applies to connectivity outages as well as planned system maintenance windows.

Please note that no patient-specific information should be included in any follow-up emails about individual cases — use appointment slot references or case numbers when coordinating across teams.

Questions about the payer list or affected codes can go to [billing contact]. Scheduling workflow questions can go to [operations contact].

Thank you for your flexibility as we work through this transition.

[Your Name]
[Title]
[Contact Information]

criteria.justification: The first substantive paragraph leads with patient experience impact — appointments needing two extra business days, same-day scheduling no longer available, and front desk flagging gaps at check-in. The operational/compliance reason (payer requirements) follows in the second paragraph, satisfying the sequencing requirement. However, while '48-hour' and 'two business days' are mentioned, there is no specific estimate of how this affects individual appointment duration or wait time at the visit level (e.g., extra minutes per appointment), which is one dimension of quantified time impact.

The 'If the Authorization System Is Unavailable' section explicitly names the failure scenario (system down, connectivity outages, planned maintenance), provides a concrete actionable fallback (fax to payer using backup forms in the front desk binder, document fax confirmation number in paper log, flag in system as 'pending — manual auth'), and does not defer to IT or management. All three dimensions are clearly satisfied.

No patient names, initials, or identifying information appear anywhere in the draft. The email explicitly instructs staff to use appointment slot references or case numbers for coordination. No clinical details or diagnoses are mentioned. The email also proactively reminds recipients not to include patient-specific information in follow-up emails, reinforcing the non-secure channel treatment.

The scheduling process is presented as exactly 5 numbered steps, meeting the cap requirement. The fallback procedure is described in prose rather than additional numbered steps, keeping the numbered list clean. No process exceeds 5 steps, and the complexity level appears appropriate for email rather than requiring a deferred training session.

dealbreaker_violations: No follow-up mechanism mentioned — the change is communicated once with no reference to a follow-up session, check-in, or reminder

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Never names patients — uses case numbers or room-style references
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: No patient names appear anywhere. The email explicitly instructs: 'use appointment slot references or case numbers when coordinating across teams' and warns against including 'case details in email.'

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Impact on patient flow presented FIRST, before operational reason
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: The opening paragraph leads with scheduling impact ('appointments that previously could be booked within the same week may now need an additional two business days') and patient experience ('same-day scheduling for these procedures will no longer be available'). The payer-driven operational reason follows in the second paragraph.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Fallback procedure included for when technology/process fails
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: Dedicated 'If the Authorization System Is Unavailable' section with fax backup, paper log documentation, and flagging instructions. Covers both unplanned outages and planned maintenance.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Numbered steps for multi-action processes, capped at 5
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: The 'Updated Scheduling Process' uses exactly 5 numbered steps, fitting within the cap.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Balances medical and administrative staff audiences / doesn't assume uniform technical literacy
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: The email references procedure codes and system names that clinical staff would know, while also giving concrete instructions for front desk staff. However, it could do slightly more to bridge the gap — e.g., briefly explaining what pre-authorization means for less experienced admin staff.

hidden_pref_satisfaction.preference: Follow-up mechanism for process changes (not communicated only once)
hidden_pref_satisfaction.evidence: There is no mention of a follow-up email, training session, check-in meeting, or any mechanism to revisit the change after initial rollout. This is a dealbreaker per the stated preferences.
